analysis.one_liner: Doubles fines on hospitals that hide their standard prices from the public.
analysis.headline: The bill, which doubles the daily fines hospitals can face for not publishing their standard prices and requires publication of a list of noncompliant hospitals, has not moved since its introduction: no cosponsors, no committee vote, no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires hospitals to publish a list of the standard prices they charge for items and services, but the maximum fines are small. This bill roughly doubles those fines (for example, from $5,500 to $11,000 per day for the largest hospitals), bans hospitals from coding their webpages so search engines can't find the price lists, and requires the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to publish a public list of every hospital that isn't complying. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone shopping for medical care. Hospital price lists that are actually published and findable online let people compare prices before getting care and make it easier for employers, researchers, and journalists to spot overcharging. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, since Medicare and Medicaid payments are benchmarked against commercial prices.

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the maximum daily civil fines for hospitals that fail to publish and update their standard charge lists: to $600 per day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds, $20 per bed per day for hospitals with 31 to 550 beds, and $11,000 per day for hospitals with more than 550 beds.
Prohibits hospitals from shielding their required price information from online search results through webpage coding, so the lists must actually be findable.
Requires the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to publish, every 180 days, the name of each hospital that is not in compliance, creating public pressure on violators.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which face doubled fines for noncompliance, potential reputational damage from being named publicly as violators, and the cost of building and maintaining accurate public price files. To the extent transparency pushes prices down, hospitals' revenue from privately insured patients could fall.

drawbacks.text: The doubled fines are still small relative to hospital revenues: a maximum of $11,000 per day is a rounding error for a large hospital system, so the bill improves enforcement at the margins but does not fundamentally change hospitals' incentive to keep negotiated prices opaque.

Publishing standard charges does not by itself guarantee patients pay less: most insured patients' costs are set by negotiated rates with insurers, and the largest fines target only the failure to post the list, not overcharging.
Small rural hospitals with thin margins bear a compliance burden along with the higher fines, which supporters would need to weigh against the public benefit of the price lists.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but modest: better enforcement of a transparency rule makes hospital prices easier to find and compare, which can help people shop for care and helps expose large price differences. The costs fall on hospitals, mostly as compliance work and fines only when they are not complying. The main limitation is design: even doubled, the fines are small enough for large hospital systems to absorb, and transparency of standard charges does not directly lower the negotiated prices most insured patients actually face. A worthwhile incremental fix rather than a solution to high hospital prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no committee vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced the bill on February 25, 2025.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill has had no further action in committee or on the floor since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet. Hospitals that do not post their standard prices are better off so far, because the current lower fines and the absence of a public violator list remain in place.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral at introduction and has taken no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so there is no record yet of how support or opposition splits by party.

industries.note: The bill doubles the daily fines hospitals can face for not publishing their standard charge lists, bars them from hiding those lists from search engines, and publicly names violators. Hospitals' interest runs against patients here: opaque pricing lets them charge more, and the transparency regime threatens that.
Published hospital charges give insurers better data for negotiating rates with hospitals and give employers buying coverage more leverage. Insurers are not regulated by this bill.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, no cosponsors, and no committee action more than a year into the Congress, the bill is unlikely to advance unless the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee schedules it or price-transparency enforcement draws renewed attention. Most bills referred to committee without cosponsors never receive a vote.
